nodes.body: The house clearance on Perch Lane filled three tables outside in the drizzle. Other people's things were laid out for anyone to buy. In a shoebox of odd items lay a tin whistle. Its mouthpiece had turned dull green with age. When tilted just right, the barrel showed six small marks scratched into the metal. A wavy line ran beneath them.

nodes.body: Inside the case was a card folded into eighths, soft as cloth, with spidery ink reading THE ROUNDS. Below that were six place names, and half of them belonged to a part of Padgett that barely still stood. The last name was BANDSTAND. A row of six numbers ran along the bottom, and four of them were crossed out. Mrs Okonjo, who ran the clearance, said the box had come from the house on Perch Lane, where a man once played in the old town band.

nodes.body: Mrs Okonjo had cleared eleven houses in Padgett that year. She remembered every single one. The paperwork for this house sat in a folder in the van. It said the house had belonged to a man named Harold Vine. He had died back in March. One box of his things had never been priced. It still waited at the bottom of the van. Every other thing that could have proved anything was gone for good.

nodes.body: Nineteen people came to the first practice in the school hall. Eleven of them had never held an instrument before. The noise was truly terrible. Bill Hurst sat at the front with his stick between his knees. He said it was just how the last one had started too.

ending.title: The Padgett Town Band, Second Time

nodes.body: A board went up inside the bandstand roof, with twenty-one names on it from 1961 and eleven from 1998, and the two lists shared four names between them. People stopped and read it, which was really the entire point of writing anything on a board at all.

The name in the cornet case belonged to a grandmother who lived on the next street. She had played until she was nineteen. She had not told anyone about it in fifty years. She took the case back. After two weeks, she brought it along to a practice.

ending.title: A Cornet Case With a Name In It

nodes.body: Two copies, one signature each, a list of eleven items, and a date, done on a Tuesday evening in the school hall with the residents watching. It was the least dramatic twenty minutes of the whole fortnight, and the only reason none of it came apart later.

There was a minute book from 1934, four hundred photographs, a run of programmes, and one card headed THE ROUNDS. All of it was recorded, numbered, and placed on a shelf. Every sheet had a date stamp on the back. Aisha put the whistle photograph in the case by the door.

Deniz left the plate uncovered and moved the menu board a foot to the left. For about a month, people came into the chip shop just to look at the piece of brass, buying chips while they were there. Then they stopped coming for that reason, but the plate stayed.

ending.title: The Plate Under the Menu Board

nodes.body: The story ran on Friday. It had a photo of an empty store and a skip. It was well written, but it told about something that had already happened. Four people wrote in afterward. They said they would have helped, if only someone had asked on Tuesday.

There were eleven players, one borrowed drum, a photocopied map, and six brass plates. The band stopped at all six spots. They played badly at every one. More people followed along than anyone expected. Half of them were under twelve.

Forty people walked the route on a Saturday in October. They followed an eighty-four-year-old man. He stopped at each plate and told what had once stood there. At the weighbridge, there was no plate at all. Everyone still stood in the car park and listened.

Five plates went back onto five walls, with the right screws. A man on the industrial estate made the sixth plate new, out of brass. He would not take any money for it. The new plate went up on the car park wall. It filled the empty rectangle that had waited twenty-eight years.

ending.title: Six Plates Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: The whistle went back into its case. The card, folded into eighths, sat beside it. It lived on a shelf and got played badly about once a week. It was the only object in the whole story that ended up right where it started. But now it meant something completely different.

ending.title: The Whistle Goes Back in Its Case

nodes.body: Instruments to the school, paper to the library, the photograph to the almshouses, plates back on the walls, and the card into the archive, with a note saying who had found it. It took three weeks of small, dull errands, and nothing was left in a bag under anybody's bed.

The store came out onto the grass. It got listed, photographed, and sorted into two piles: keep and skip. Two men, paid by the hour, watched. They turned out to be surprisingly interested. By the end of the week, the room under the bandstand was swept, dry, and empty.

The skip left the park at nine on Friday morning. It carried a bass drum and four cases inside. Someone took a photo of it leaving, from the gate. The Gazette would not print the photo. There was simply nothing to say about it.

Three different adults would have stopped it, but no one told them. Asking had felt like a big deal on Wednesday, yet by the next Monday, it did not feel so important. All three adults admitted this, one after another.

The last order was wrong, and the wheels went back to zero. The trail had started with a shoebox in Perch Lane, and it ran through six walls and sixty years. Now it ended at a steel door in a cold park, with a lorry booked for the morning.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
